content.summary_of_the_paper: Supervised ViTs often have scattered, noisy attention maps. To address this issue, the authors propose to add a spatial entropy regularization during training, which first groups the attention map into different regions (objects), and then penalize the number and uniform distribution of objects via minimizing the spatial entropy. The authors show that the method can push ViTs to have cleaner attention maps. They also propose to remove the MSA skip connection in the last layer, further promoting the performance. Experiments are conducted on image classifcation on ImageNet and robustness benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ The motivation is clear and the method is intuitively sensible.

+ The paper is easy to follow.

- The entropy will penalize the uniformity of attention distribution. However, what if there are multiple objects in the image and attention should be evenly allocated on each object (like the example in Figure 2)? Will SAR push the model to only attend to one single object in this case?

- Have the authors try to add SAR in every layer of ViT (or the last few layers)? Will it further boost the classification accuracy and robustness?

- I'm not sure I fully understand why the arguments for removing the MSA skip connection in Section 4.2 are related to SAR. The first reason, put forward by the authors, is that the skip connection will propagate the tokens in previous layer into the final layer, thus the residual token embeddings in the last layer are ignored, which is detrimental to the performance. To my understanding, isn't that what skip connections are designed for, i.e., to pass the output from previous layer and let the current layer only learn the residual (which could be small in higher layers)? I do not understand why this will harm the performance. The second argument is that adding the skip connection will make the effective receptive filed smaller, but I'm not sure why smaller receptive field will lead to inferior results. Is it because the receptive field cannot cover the whole object? It would be helpful if the authors can show the attention map before and after removing the skip connections.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall the presentation is clear, although more explanations are needed in Section 4.2. The method is sensible and easy enough to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a effective method to purify ViTs' attention maps, although some arguments need more clarification.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: With self-supervised approaches, the attention maps of vision transformers are generally dense and allow to have a relatively good "segmentation" of the main object  in the image. However, with supervised approaches this is generally not the case because the attention maps focus on discriminating parts of the objects. The paper proposes a regularization method to solve this "issue". The method is evaluated on image classification tasks on the following datasets: ImageNet (1k and 100 labels), CIFAR-10. CIFAR-100, Flowers, Pets and segmentation tasks on ADE20k (in appendix) and Pascal VoC.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

- Idea:The proposed idea is interesting and can be very useful especially for weakly semantic segmentation even if this aspect is not the main focus of the paper
- Evaluation: The paper considered different evaluation settup which is a good practice however the evaluations are not very extensive (see weakness)

- Results: The results seem good especially for segmentation and small scale dataset.

Weaknesses:

- Model size: The experiments are done with small models, it would be interesting to evaluate it with larger models that usually require more regularization to see how the method generalizes.

- Standard deviation: The standard deviation is not reported in the different evaluation protocols. This makes it more difficult to interpret the results, especially for ablation. It is difficult to know if the impact of the proposed method is significant.

- Overfitting evaluation: The ImageNet dataset does not have a separate validation and test set so it is important to add evaluation on ImageNet-v2 [1] to measure the level of overfitting.

[1] Recht et al., Do ImageNet Classifiers Generalize to ImageNet?

- Training costs: It would be interesting to add an evaluation of the training cost of using the proposed method.

- Comparison with other self-supervised approach for image classification on small scale datasets: It seems that on larger scale evaluations like ImageNet the impact of the method is quite limited. However, the method gives improvements on smaller datasets. It has been shown that approaches that combine self-supervised and supervised learning [1] with ViT architectures are better on small datasets. It would be interesting to add a comparison with other self-supervised approaches to know if the improvement are linked to the proposed approach and not only to the self-supervised aspect.

[1] El-Nouby et al., Are Large-scale Datasets Necessary for Self-Supervised Pre-training?

- Architectures used: Most of the ablation and experimentation other than on ImageNet-1k are done with ViT-S only, it would be necessary to add results with other architecture to see if the method generalizes or not.

Suggestion:
- The segmentation aspects of the proposed method are really interesting. It would strengthen the paper a lot to have experiments that show that it works with different architectures of different sizes (Not only ViT-S and PVT-S) on Pascale Voc and ADE20k.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well written and easy to follow, the method is new and the results are quite interesting even if the experimental part needs to be reinforced on some points. The code is provided in appendix so the results will be reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The proposed method is simple and interesting. The results seem to be good especially in segmentation. However, it is necessary to reinforce the experimental part in order to completely validate the method.


====== Post rebuttal ====

As there is no rebuttal the different issues raised in the reviews are not resolved. So I will lower my original score and tend to reject the paper.  However, I believe that by incorporating the various remarks raised in the reviews it is possible to have a very interesting paper.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a simple regularizer for ViT that makes attention more object-centric. To this end, the proposed spatial attention-based regularization (SAR) finds the connected components of patches based on the similarity to the [CLS] token. Then, SAR reinforces the patches in the same component to increase the similarity, giving attention have better visualization and improving object recognition. The efficacy of SAR is validated on various ViT architectures and training scenarios.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength

- The proposed method is simple and effective.
- The method can be applied to arbitrary ViT architectures, including DeiT, T2T, PVT, and CvT.
- The paper does an extensive experiments: supervised learning, transfer learning, and OOD generalization. I also appreciate the self-supervised learning and semantic segmentation results in Appendix.


### Weekness

**Multi-object images**

The paper only considers (single-object) iconic images as a training dataset. Thus, most images may have a single connected component. Can SAR be applied for multi-object images like COCO? It would be challenging since now the attention should discriminate all small objects in the scene. To verify this, the authors ci show improvements in object detection, improving the vanilla ViTDet [1] benchmark.

p.s. Providing a histogram for the number of connected components would be informative, using the models trained on ImageNet-1K and multi-object (e.g., COCO) dataset.

[1] Li et al. Exploring Plain Vision Transformer Backbones for Object Detection. arXiv 2022.

**Mixup and CutMix**

Popular training schemes (e.g., the default of DeiT) often use mixup-like augmentations combining two samples. How can one infer connected components from them? Can the method be compatible with Mixup and CutMix?

**Longer training results**

In Figure 3, the gain of SAR is okay in early epochs, but the gap decreases as the training goes. The gain seems pretty marginal at the final 300 epoch, yet the training curve is not fully saturated. What would happen if we train a longer epoch until both models converge? The gap may be decreased, perhaps cross-over later.

**Comparison with other baselines**

SAR is basically a token-level regularizer that makes similar tokens more similar. While the motivation is different, one may apply TokenLabeling (using an unsupervised attention map $\approx$ object label as the target) [1] or SelfPatch (although the paper targetted self-supervised learning, the objective can also be used for supervised learning) [2]. Discussing the difference with them and comparing the performance would be informative.

On the other hand, there is a line of work about object-centric learning. For example, GENESIS-v2 [3] considers somewhat similar inductive bias clustering the features in the neighborhood. OSRT [4] applies a Slot Attention [5] to cluster the same object and decompose the scene. ORViT [6] and ReMixer [7] considers more modern ViT architectures, although they leverage pretrained object detector, unlike a simple regularizer of SAR. Adding related work may help future readers to understand the historical context.


[1] Jiang et al. All Tokens Matter: Token Labeling for Training Better Vision Transformers. NeurIPS 2021.\
[2] Yun et al. Patch-Level Representation Learning for Self-Supervised Vision Transformers. CVPR 2022.\
[3] Engelcke et al. GENESIS-V2: Inferring Unordered Object Representations without Iterative Refinement. NeurIPS 2021.\
[4] Sajjadi et al. Object Scene Representation Transformer. NeurIPS 2022.\
[5] Locatello et al. Object-Centric Learning with Slot Attention. NeurIPS 2020.\
[6] Herzig et al. Object-Region Video Transformers. CVPR 2022.\
[7] Kang et al. ReMixer: Object-aware Mixing Layer for Vision Transformers and Mixers. ICLRW 2022.


**Computation cost for training**

How much SAR increases the training time? Finding connected components can be a bottleneck depending on the choice of algorithm.

**Contextual and background bias**

The object-centric learning may improve the robustness on contextual [1] and background [2] bias. Evaluating the performance of SAR on those datasets would be informative.

[1] Liang & Zou. MetaShift: A Dataset of Datasets for Evaluating Contextual Distribution Shifts and Training Conflicts. ICLR 2022.\
[2] Xiao et al. Noise or Signal: The Role of Image Backgrounds in Object Recognition. ICLR 2021.

**Hook figure**

Figure 1 is not attractive enough. Why should the reflection in the lake be considered the same object? Is it the best example? Since the hook figure would be the one cherry-picked, the superiority of SAR over DINO is not convincing.

Editorial comments
- The paper mixes the terminoligy "VT" and "ViT"
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Good.
Quality: Good, yet experiments could be further strengthened.
Novelty: Okay.
Reproducibility: Code is submitted.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, I think the proposed method is simple and effective. However, I think the paper could strengthen its impact if it verifies the effectiveness in more diverse scenarios. I'm happy to raise the score if my concerns are addressed:
- Multi-object image experiments (e.g., object detection)
- Compatibility with Mixup and CutMix
- Longer training results for Figure 3
- Comparison with other baselines
- Computation cost for training
- Robustness on contextual and background bias
- (minor) revise Figure 1

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to add inductive bias to the last layer attention map that encouraging low spatial entropies, which is computed with connected components of the spatial attention map. The main motivation is that attention maps should be focusing on few connected regions instead of spreading the whole image. Experiments are conducted on ImageNet, ImageNet-100, and some downstream classification tasks to validate its performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: It proposes a novel spatial entropy formulation with attention maps and with the proposed loss, ViT trained in supervised way can have similar segmentation capability as in previous self-supervised ViT (DINO).

	Weaknesses:	The experiments part is not convincing enough to support the proposed method. 
1.	In table 1 (b), is F: A+SAR equivalent to C + spatial entropy loss? Can authors show model C and model F comparison in Table 1 (c) as well? Want to check how much gain comes from removing skip-connection and LN. 
2.	Only last layer attention map is used and regularized, can authors shed light on this design? Can authors give some empirical results ablating where/which layers to add this regularization?
3.	From Table 2, the proposed method only gives little gain when the models are already large/well-optimized, e.g. 0.04 for PVT, 0.2 for CvT. Besides, the gain comes from removing skip connection, LN, adding spatial entropy loss altogether, the actual gain from spatial entropy loss might even be smaller. Can authors also show separate gain with those changing for full ImageNet results?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity is good, novelty is marginal and reproducibility is good as proposed method is simple.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper proposes an interesting way to add inductive object bias to vision transformers. However, current experiments results do not fully support the method. The results shows marginal improvement, and is coming with other changes that bring gain as well (removing skip connections, LN). Critical ablation studies are missing and the performance gain is limited when applying to vision transformers other than small vanilla ViTs.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
